BBC News — published 24 September 2026 09:47 BST (08:47 UTC), updated 14:07 BST

HEADLINE: County Durham and Darlington NHS Foundation Trust agrees to review up to 4,500 more breast cancer cases, extending the lookback to 2015.

FACTS (BBC):
- Board held an extraordinary meeting in Durham on Thursday and agreed to extend the breast surgery lookback review one year at a time back to 2015 — up to 4,500 further cases, estimated to take five years.
- Existing review began April 2025, covering January 2023 to February 2025. Of 538 cases reviewed so far, 321 involved some form of harm, including one death.
- About 640 patients have contacted a special helpline asking for their cases to be reviewed.
- The review cost about £523,000 in its first year, with nine reviewers examining about 80 cases a month.
- Chief nurse Gill Hunt said concerns were first raised in 2015 after a "service reconfiguration" and loss of breast surgical trainee posts; key themes were treatment "not aligned to best practice", excessive surgery and delayed diagnosis.
- Some women who had unnecessary mastectomies may be offered reconstruction surgery.

QUOTES:
Alison Marshall, trust board chair: "I would like to offer a sincere apology to all the women and their families who have been affected by the failings in our breast services. I can't imagine the impact that has had." She said they could "not turn back the clock" but would be "open, honest and transparent".
Steve Russell, chief executive: the trust was "incredibly conscious women and their families" had experienced "distress, uncertainty and harm"; patients today could be "confident" they would be "treated appropriately".
Denise Howarth, 51, of Consett, who had an unnecessary mastectomy: said she was "pleased" the review would be extended; past patients need to be contacted with "dignity" and "compassion"; she wants a public inquiry and a look-back beyond 2015 (her case dates to 2012).
Rachel Gray, 41, Sunderland: the review found she could have avoided a mastectomy at 37 — discovering that made her "want to crawl out of my skin".
Chloe Gibson, medical negligence solicitor: the process would be "very long" and last until the 2030s; "Justice delayed is justice denied"; a full public inquiry is the "only way proper scrutiny and full accountability can be achieved".

HOUSEHOLD ANGLE: NHS cancer care quality; helpline remains open to any past patient irrespective of when treated.
